newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler warns U.S. no compromise on food safety.
newsitem.headline: Fischler warns U.S. no compromise on food safety.

text.p: European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler warned on Tuesday the European Union was prepared to face a trade row with the United States rather than compromise on the safety standards of EU meat and poultry.
"Seeing as we are dealing with the health of the consumer no compromise can be struck," Fischler told the European Parliament's agriculture committee.

The U.S. announced earlier on Tuesday it would postpone until April 30 a threatened ban on EU meat and poultry imports in the hope that further transatlantic talks could end a three-year dispute on veterinary standards.

Washington had said that if no deal were reached by Tuesday it would remove more than 100 European meat and poultry plants from its approved exporters list. Such an action could halt up to $300 million worth of EU meat shipments to the U.S., mostly pork products from Denmark and ham from Italy.
At issue in the dispute are veterinary inspections of imported animal products.
Fischler welcomed the Americans' decision and said he hoped a European Commission team travelling to Washington on Wednesday could strike a compromise with the Americans.
But he warned Brussels was not prepared to accept a deal which meant compromising on food safety and he deplored the U.S. attempt to change the EU's mind with trade sanction threats.

"Threats of this sort cannot force us to toe the line and the U.S. will have to take the consequences of such an unjustified and disproportionate measure," Fischler told his audience to loud applause.
The 15-member EU was prepared to face a row with Washington at the World Trade Organisation if that was necessary to protect European consumers, the Austrian commissioner stressed.
Fischler said EU food hygiene rules required meat and poultry products to be safe at all stages of production "from the farmyard to the table".

European veterinary experts thought the American practice of simply treating animal carcasses with chlorine-based chemicals to rid them of any unhygienic elements picked up along the way was "dubious from the health point of view," he said.
On April 1, the EU brought in new rules which U.S. officials say block $100 million-worth of U.S. exports to Europe.

The new rules were introduced after the two sides failed to reach agreement in talks which began three years ago after the end of the Uruguay Round of negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
